title: Agreeing the transition plan & transferring risk
blurb: Explain how to engage stakeholders to agree a transition plan, what it contains, and how open risks and issues are transferred to BAU owners.
question: A water company's smart-meter project is two months from closing. Customer services, field operations, IT support and the meter supplier all have a stake in go-live, and several project risks are still open. How should the project manager reach an agreed transition plan, and what must happen to those open risks?

teach.h: A plan the receivers sign up to
teach.body: The transition plan sets out how the outputs will move into business as usual: timing, responsibilities, readiness checks, acceptance, support arrangements and the transfer of risks and issues to BAU owners. It must be AGREED with stakeholders through engagement and consultation, not imposed. In plain English: the people who will live with the outputs help shape the handover, so they're committed to it and nothing they need is forgotten.

teach.h: Who needs to agree the plan, and why
head: Stakeholder
Their stake in transition
rows: Accepts the outputs; ensures BAU is ready; owns benefits
Must adopt the outputs and work in the new way
Will run the outputs and own ongoing risks
Will fix faults and answer queries after go-live
teach.caption: Each group holds part of what makes transition work. Leave one out and a gap appears.

teach.h: Transfer of risks: nothing left unowned
teach.body: When the project closes, the team disbands and the project's risk register stops being managed. Any risk or issue still open must be handed to a named BAU owner who understands it, accepts it and has a response to carry out. That transfer has to be negotiated, not dumped: owners need to know the risk, its triggers and the agreed actions. Otherwise risks become orphaned and, when they occur, nobody acts.

rows.label: Risk transfer
values: Mostly at the end, in one go
Incrementally, as each release goes live

teach.text: Don't confuse 'transfer of risks' at transition with the TRANSFER risk response. The response 'transfer' passes a threat to a third party (insurance, contract). Transition risk transfer hands ownership of open project risks to BAU owners inside the organisation. Also wrong: 'the PM keeps the risks after closure' (the PM leaves) and 'close all risks so none are open' (that hides them).

teach.body: A plan drafted alone and emailed a week before go-live misses things only BAU knows: rota patterns, peak periods, system freezes, real support capacity. Operations managers who weren't consulted feel no ownership and may resist, and risk owners refuse risks they don't understand. Engagement takes longer up front but produces a plan that's realistic, accepted and actually followed.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Name the stakeholders: sponsor, users, BAU and operations managers, support teams, suppliers.
Explain engagement: analyse, consult, involve, resolve conflicts, then agree and communicate.
List the plan's contents: timing, responsibilities, readiness checks, acceptance, support, risks and issues.
Explain risk transfer: open risks and issues handed to named BAU owners who accept them.
Give the reason: ownership and buy-in, so nothing is left unowned after the project closes.
The transition plan is agreed with stakeholders through engagement, not imposed.
Key stakeholders: sponsor, users, BAU and operations managers, support teams, suppliers.
Contents: timing, responsibilities, readiness checks, acceptance, support, transfer of risks and issues.
Open risks AND issues go to named BAU owners who understand and accept them.
The sponsor accepts the outputs and ensures BAU is ready; the PM hands over and closes.

summary: You can now explain how to engage stakeholders to agree a transition plan and what that plan contains. You can also explain why open risks and issues must be transferred to named BAU owners, and how this differs between linear and iterative projects.

A.q: Why should a transition plan be agreed with stakeholders rather than imposed by the project manager?
options: So the PM avoids accountability for it
So readiness checks can be skipped
So those running the outputs commit to it
So the suppliers can choose the go-live date
A.why: Engaging those who will run and support the outputs builds commitment and surfaces knowledge the PM lacks.

whyNot.0: The PM remains responsible for handing over; agreement doesn't remove that.
whyNot.1: Readiness checks are part of the plan, not something agreement replaces.
whyNot.3: Go-live timing is agreed with the business, especially BAU, not chosen by suppliers.

A.q: In a transition plan, what does 'transfer of risks' mean?
options: Passing a threat to an insurer
Closing every risk before handover
Moving risks from the sponsor to the PM
Handing open risks to named BAU owners
A.why: Open project risks are handed to BAU owners who understand them, accept them and carry out the agreed responses.

whyNot.0: That is the 'transfer' risk response, which involves a third party.
whyNot.1: Closing risks that are still live hides them rather than managing them.
whyNot.2: The PM leaves at closure, so risks must go to BAU owners.

A.q: Which group is MOST important to consult on the go-live date of a new call-centre system?
options: The call-centre operations managers
The project's own planning team
The supplier's finance department
The organisation's external auditors
A.why: Operations managers know BAU peaks, rotas and capacity, so the go-live date must work for them.

whyNot.1: The planning team schedules the work but doesn't know BAU constraints first-hand.
whyNot.2: Supplier finance has no say in operational timing.
whyNot.3: Auditors provide assurance; they don't set operational dates.

B.q:
Which TWO items would you expect to find in a transition plan?
1) Support arrangements after go-live
2) Tender evaluation criteria
3) Readiness checks and acceptance
4) The team's Belbin role profiles
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Support arrangements and readiness checks with acceptance are core contents of a transition plan.

whyNot.0: Tender criteria belong to procurement, not transition.
whyNot.2: Neither tender criteria nor Belbin profiles belong in a transition plan.
whyNot.3: Readiness checks belong, but Belbin profiles are about team roles.

B.q: The IT service manager refuses to accept an open risk about system slowdowns at peak times. What is the BEST next step?
options: Close the risk so it no longer shows
Discuss it and agree a response and owner
Keep it on the project register for good
Remove the manager from the transition plan
B.why: Risk transfer must be negotiated: explain the risk, agree a workable response and confirm who will own it.

whyNot.0: Closing a live risk hides it; it will still happen.
whyNot.2: The project register stops being managed once the project closes.
whyNot.3: Excluding the person who must own the risk makes the gap worse.

B.q: An iterative project releases a new increment every quarter. How is its transition plan MOST likely handled?
options: Agreed and updated for each release
Agreed once and never revisited
Written only after the last release
Left entirely to the supplier
B.why: Each release is a transition into BAU, so the plan is agreed and updated release by release, with risks transferred incrementally.

whyNot.1: Each release brings new readiness needs and risks, so the plan must be revisited.
whyNot.2: Earlier releases would go live with no agreed plan.
whyNot.3: The business and BAU owners must agree the plan, not just the supplier.

C.q: Six weeks after a project closes, an open risk about data migration errors occurs. Nobody acts because nobody owns it. What failed?
options: Risks weren't transferred to BAU owners
The risk wasn't entered in the change log
The success criteria were set too high
The supplier's contract was fixed price
C.why: Open risks must be handed to named BAU owners at transition so someone carries out the response after the project closes.

whyNot.1: Risks go in the risk register; the change log records change requests.
whyNot.2: Success criteria don't decide who owns risks after closure.
whyNot.3: The contract type doesn't explain why no internal owner acted.

C.q: A project manager drafts a transition plan alone, then emails it to operations a week before go-live. Which outcome is MOST likely?
options: Faster acceptance, as it saved meetings
Low buy-in and gaps the PM didn't see
Stronger ownership by operations
Fewer risks to hand over at closure
C.why: Without engagement, operations feel no ownership and the plan misses BAU knowledge such as peaks, rotas and capacity.

whyNot.0: Skipping engagement usually slows acceptance because of objections and rework.
whyNot.2: Ownership comes from involvement, which this approach lacks.
whyNot.3: The number of open risks doesn't fall because the plan was written alone.

C.q: Which is NOT a good reason to involve suppliers in agreeing the transition plan?
options: They may provide warranty and support
They hold knowledge BAU will need
They may own defects still to be fixed
They are accountable for the benefits
C.why: Benefits are the sponsor's accountability, with benefit owners in the business; suppliers deliver and support outputs.

whyNot.0: Warranty and support arrangements are a key part of the plan.
whyNot.1: Supplier knowledge often needs transferring to BAU.
whyNot.2: Open defects are issues that must be owned and scheduled for fixing.

reteach.title: Passing the baton in a relay
reteach.question: In a relay race, the baton must pass from one runner to the next without being dropped. What does a good baton change teach us about agreeing a transition plan and transferring risk?

blocks.body: Relay teams practise the change together: they agree the marker where the next runner starts, the call, and the hand. The incoming runner doesn't let go until the receiver has a firm grip. A project is the incoming runner; BAU is the receiver. The plan is agreed together beforehand, and risks are only 'let go' when a named BAU owner has a firm grip on them.

blocks.text: Throwing the baton from ten metres away is an imposed plan. It might arrive, but it will probably be dropped.

explain.body: Timing, responsibilities, readiness checks, acceptance, support arrangements, and the transfer of risks and issues to BAU owners.

test.q: Which item belongs in a transition plan?
options: The weighting of tender criteria
The original feasibility study
Who does each handover task
Team members' individual pay
test.why: Responsibilities for handover tasks are a core part of the transition plan.

whyNot.0: Tender criteria are part of procurement.
whyNot.1: The feasibility study is an early-phase document.

explain.body: Sponsor, users, BAU and operations managers, support teams and suppliers. At transition the PM hands over and closes; the sponsor accepts the outputs and makes sure BAU is ready.

test.q: Who formally accepts the outputs and makes sure BAU is ready at transition?
options: The supplier
The project office
The project team
The sponsor
test.why: The sponsor accepts the outputs and ensures the business is ready; the PM hands over and closes.

whyNot.0: The supplier delivers outputs; it doesn't accept them for the business.
whyNot.1: A project office supports and assures, but doesn't accept outputs.
whyNot.2: The team delivers the outputs and then disbands.

explain.body: Use stakeholder analysis, then consult and involve: draft the plan with BAU in workshops, resolve conflicts (such as go-live timing) and confirm agreement.

test.q: Which approach BEST engages operations managers in the transition plan?
options: Sending them the final plan for information
Consulting them only if problems arise
Leaving them out to keep the plan simple
Workshops where they help shape the plan
test.why: Involving operations managers in shaping the plan builds ownership and brings in BAU knowledge.

whyNot.0: Informing alone is the lowest level of engagement.
whyNot.1: Waiting for problems means gaps are found too late.

explain.body: Open risks and unresolved issues are handed to named BAU owners, with their responses, through discussion and agreement, so nothing is left unowned after closure.

test.q: As well as open risks, what else should be handed to BAU owners at transition?
options: Open issues
Decision gates
Team timesheets
The project budget
test.why: Unresolved issues, like open risks, need named BAU owners so they are dealt with after the project closes.

whyNot.1: Decision gates are project governance points and end with the project.
whyNot.3: The project budget is closed down; ongoing costs move to BAU budgets.
